content: The Surveillance Guide for Vaccine-Preventable Diseases in the WHO South-East Asia Region: Japanese Encephalitis (September 2023) provides detailed guidance on the surveillance and management of Japanese Encephalitis (JE), a disease caused by the JE virus. This virus is primarily transmitted through Culex mosquito species and maintained in a zoonotic cycle involving animals such as pigs and birds (e.g., herons, egrets). JE is the leading cause of viral encephalitis in Asia, and human vaccination has been identified as the most effective preventive measure. Translations must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the accuracy of the translation. Surveillance Objectives The primary objectives of JE surveillance are: 1. To understand the epidemiology of JE, including identifying at-risk populations and estimating the disease burden. 2. To determine the geographical distribution of JE within a country. 3. To provide data for the development of vaccination policies. 4. To evaluate the impact and effectiveness of vaccination programs after their implementation. Surveillance Methods 1. Sentinel Hospital-Based Surveillance: This is recommended in areas where JE is suspected to be a public health issue. Sentinel sites should initially include hospitals with the highest number of suspected cases and can be expanded as needed. These sites should ideally be located in JE-endemic areas and serve as referral centers for encephalitis patients. The capability of the health facility to conduct active case detection and specimen collection is also a key consideration. 2. Nationwide Case-Based Surveillance: This approach is resource-intensive but provides comprehensive data on the disease burden. It involves laboratory confirmation of all suspected cases and is particularly useful in countries with high levels of JE control. 3. Age Group Surveillance: Surveillance is recommended for all age groups, as JE can affect older populations, especially in areas where the virus is newly introduced or where vaccination programs have shifted the burden to unvaccinated older individuals. However, in countries in the early stages of JE vaccination programs, focusing on children under 15 years of age may be more cost-effective. Case Detection and Definition A suspected JE case is defined as a person of any age who develops acute fever and at least one of the following: A change in mental status (e.g., confusion, disorientation, coma, or inability to talk). New onset of seizures, excluding simple febrile seizures. Simple febrile seizures are defined as single generalized convulsions lasting less than 15 minutes in children aged 6 months to 6 years, with no other findings except fever, and recovery of consciousness within 60 minutes. The case definition for Acute Encephalitis Syndrome (AES) has high sensitivity but low specificity. It captures approximately two-thirds of JE cases in children and has 100% sensitivity in adults, though the sample size for adults is smaller. Clinical Presentation JE typically begins with sudden-onset fever, headache, and vomiting. In children, gastrointestinal symptoms may dominate initially. Over the next few days, changes in mental status, focal neurological deficits, generalized weakness, and movement disorders may develop. Classical JE symptoms include a mask-like face, tremors, muscular stiffness, and involuntary movements (choreoathetosis). Acute flaccid paralysis, resembling poliomyelitis, has also been associated with JE. Seizures are common, particularly in children. Specimen Collection and Laboratory Testing 1. Preferred Specimens: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) obtained via lumbar puncture is the preferred specimen for laboratory confirmation of JE. JE virus-specific IgM antibodies can be detected in CSF by the fourth day of symptom onset. If lumbar puncture is not feasible, blood samples should be collected for testing. 2. Sample Volume: CSF: At least two tubes for microbiological analysis (Gram stain, bacterial culture) and estimation of glucose, protein, and cell count. Blood: 3–5 mL for older children and adults; 1–2 mL for infants and younger children. 3. Storage and Transport: For transport within 1–3 days, store CSF and serum samples at 2–8°C. For longer storage, freeze samples at or below -20°C. Avoid repeated freezing and thawing. 4. Second Blood Sample: If the first sample is negative for JE IgM, a second sample should be collected on day 10 of illness, at discharge, or at the time of death. Laboratory Confirmation The recommended method for laboratory confirmation is the detection of JE virus-specific IgM antibodies using an IgM capture ELISA. Sensitivity increases to over 95% by 10 days after symptom onset. It is crucial to differentiate true JE infections from other flavivirus infections (e.g., dengue) that may yield false-positive results due to cross-reactivity. Validated dengue-specific assays should be performed on all JE-positive specimens to rule out false positives. Case Reporting and Investigation All suspected JE cases must be reported to the district surveillance officer. On-site healthcare staff are responsible for collecting specimens and completing a case investigation form within 48 hours of reporting. Each case should be assigned a unique identification number (UID) that includes geographical and temporal identifiers. Public Health Implications JE surveillance is essential for monitoring vaccine effectiveness, identifying high-risk areas, and guiding public health responses. Sentinel hospital-based surveillance is particularly practical in resource-limited settings, while nationwide surveillance provides comprehensive data in countries with advanced JE control.
